rows.stem: If \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^2 + 7I = kA\), then the value of k is :
rows.solution: First square the matrix: \(A^2 = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 5 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\). Then \(A^2 + 7I = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 5 \\ -5 & 10 \end{bmatrix}\), while \(kA = \begin{bmatrix} 3k & k \\ -k & 2k \end{bmatrix}\). Comparing entries gives \(3k = 15\), \(k = 5\), \(-k = -5\) and \(2k = 10\), all four agreeing on \(k = 5\).

rows.stem: Let \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & -3 \\ 3 & -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(B = \dfrac{1}{3}\begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & -3 \\ 6 & 1 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}\). If \(AB = I\), then the value of \(\lambda\) is :
rows.solution:
Write \(M = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 0 & 1 \\ 9 & 2 & -3 \\ 6 & 1 & \lambda \end{bmatrix}\), so that \(B = \dfrac{1}{3}M\), and multiply out \(AM\) row by row. For example the leading entry is \(1(-2) + (-1)(9) + 2(6) = 1\), and the bottom-right entry is \(3(1) + (-2)(-3) + 4\lambda = 9 + 4\lambda\). Altogether \(AM = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 4 + 2\lambda \\ 0 & 1 & -6 - 3\lambda \\ 0 & 0 & 9 + 4\lambda \end{bmatrix}\). Requiring \(AM = I\) gives \(4 + 2\lambda = 0\), \(-6 - 3\lambda = 0\) and \(9 + 4\lambda = 1\), and all three agree on \(\lambda = -2\); with that value \(M\) is precisely \(A^{-1}\). So the required value is \(-2\).
[Note on the question as printed: it is inconsistent. Since \(B = \dfrac{1}{3}M\), we get \(AB = \dfrac{1}{3}AM\), whose leading entry is \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) and never \(1\) — so \(AB = I\) cannot hold for ANY \(\lambda\), and the factor \(\dfrac{1}{3}\) must be a misprint. A candidate who kept the factor and matched only the bottom-right entry would solve \(\dfrac{1}{3}(9 + 4\lambda) = 1\) and reach \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\), which is one of the other choices; CBSE's marking scheme accordingly accepts either \(-2\) or \(-\dfrac{3}{2}\). The key stored here is \(-2\), the value that genuinely makes \(M = A^{-1}\).]

rows.stem: Derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x^3\), is :
rows.solution: Put \(u = x^2\) and \(v = x^3\), and use \(\dfrac{du}{dv} = \dfrac{du/dx}{dv/dx}\). Here \(\dfrac{du}{dx} = 2x\) and \(\dfrac{dv}{dx} = 3x^2\), so \(\dfrac{du}{dv} = \dfrac{2x}{3x^2} = \dfrac{2}{3x}\) (for \(x \neq 0\)). The derivative of \(x^2\) with respect to \(x^3\) is therefore \(\dfrac{2}{3x}\).

options.label: B
options.text: differentiable but not continuous at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\).

options.label: C
options.text: continuous but not differentiable at \(x = 0\) only.

options.label: D
options.text: neither continuous nor differentiable at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\).

rows.solution: A modulus function is continuous everywhere, and a sum of continuous functions is continuous, so \(f\) is continuous on all of \(R\) — in particular at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\). That rules out the two choices claiming a break. Differentiability is another matter: \(|x|\) has a corner at \(x = 0\) and \(|x - 2|\) has a corner at \(x = 2\). Writing \(f\) piecewise, \(f(x) = 2 - 2x\) for \(x < 0\), \(f(x) = 2\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\) and \(f(x) = 2x - 2\) for \(x > 2\). At \(x = 0\) the left-hand derivative is \(-2\) and the right-hand derivative is \(0\); at \(x = 2\) they are \(0\) and \(2\). The one-sided derivatives differ at both points, so \(f\) fails to be differentiable at each of them. Hence \(f\) is continuous, but not differentiable at \(x = 0\) and \(x = 2\).

rows.subtopic: Definite Integrals and the Fundamental Theorem
rows.solution: Substitute \(u = \dfrac{\theta}{3}\), so \(d\theta = 3\, du\) and the limits \(\theta = 0, \pi\) become \(u = 0, \dfrac{\pi}{3}\). Then the integral is \(3\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/3} \tan^2 u\, du\). Using \(\tan^2 u = \sec^2 u - 1\), this is \(3\int\limits_{0}^{\pi/3}(\sec^2 u - 1)\, du = 3\left[\tan u - u\right]_{0}^{\pi/3} = 3\left(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3\left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 3\sqrt{3} - \pi\). (Note the value must be positive, since \(\tan^2\) is non-negative, and \(3\sqrt{3} - \pi \approx 2.06\) indeed is.)

rows.stem: The integrating factor of the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + \dfrac{2}{x}y = 0\), \(x \neq 0\) is :
rows.solution: The equation is already in the standard linear form \(\dfrac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q\), with \(P = \dfrac{2}{x}\). The integrating factor is \(e^{\int P\, dx} = e^{\int \frac{2}{x}\, dx} = e^{2\log|x|} = e^{\log x^2} = x^2\). So the integrating factor is \(x^2\). (The choice \(e^{\log(2x)}\) simplifies to \(2x\), which is not it, and \(\dfrac{2}{x}\) is \(P\) itself rather than the integrating factor.)

rows.subtopic: Equation of a Line in Space
rows.stem: The Cartesian equation of a line passing through the point with position vector \(\vec{a} = \hat{i} - \hat{j}\) and parallel to the line \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j})\), is
rows.solution: The line passes through the point whose position vector is \(\hat{i} - \hat{j}\), that is \((1, -1, 0)\), and being parallel to \(\vec{r} = \hat{i} + \hat{k} + \mu(2\hat{i} - \hat{j})\) it has the same direction vector \(2\hat{i} - \hat{j}\), i.e. direction ratios \(\langle 2, -1, 0 \rangle\). The Cartesian form of a line through \((x_1, y_1, z_1)\) with direction ratios \(\langle a, b, c \rangle\) is \(\dfrac{x - x_1}{a} = \dfrac{y - y_1}{b} = \dfrac{z - z_1}{c}\), so here it is \(\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 1}{-1} = \dfrac{z}{0}\). (The zero denominator is the usual symbolic convention recording that \(z\) stays \(0\) along the line.)
